Psychology: clinical and health

Assessment, prevention, intervention, chronic illness and quality of life.

What it does

Clinical and health psychology assesses, prevents and treats psychological problems, from anxiety or depression to severe disorders, and helps people cope with physical illness. It starts from a simple idea: health does not depend only on the body, but also on how we think, feel, behave and relate to others. This is the biopsychosocial model proposed by the psychiatrist George Engel in 1977.

Where it works

  • Mental health centres, hospitals and clinical psychology units.
  • Primary care, alongside family doctors and nurses.
  • Pain, oncology, cardiology, diabetes or palliative care units.
  • Private practice, patient associations and prevention programmes.

What works according to research

  • Cognitive behavioural therapy for anxiety, depression, insomnia and many other problems.
  • Contextual therapies, such as acceptance and commitment therapy, especially for chronic pain.
  • Brief interventions to stop smoking, cut down on alcohol or improve adherence to treatment.
  • Psychoeducation: explaining clearly what is happening and what can be done already has measurable effects.

An example

The English programme Improving Access to Psychological Therapies, launched in 2008, offers brief evidence-based psychological therapy to people with anxiety and depression referred from primary care. It records the outcome of almost every patient, and roughly half of those who complete treatment recover. In Spain, the PsicAP trial showed that group cognitive behavioural therapy within primary care improved outcomes compared with usual treatment.

The profession in Spain

Treating health problems requires specific qualifications. The PIR route (a four-year residency in the public health system) leads to the specialist title in Clinical Psychology. The master's degree in General Health Psychology qualifies psychologists to work in private healthcare. Spain has far fewer clinical psychologists per inhabitant in public healthcare than the European average, a problem repeatedly highlighted by the Ombudsman and scientific societies.

References

  1. Engel, G. L. (1977). The need for a new medical model: A challenge for biomedicine. Science, 196(4286), 129–136.
  2. Clark, D. M. (2018). Realizing the mass public benefit of evidence-based psychological therapies: The IAPT program. Annual Review of Clinical Psychology, 14, 159–183.
  3. Cano-Vindel, A. et al. (2021). Transdiagnostic group cognitive behavioural therapy for emotional disorders in primary care: The PsicAP randomized controlled trial. Psychological Medicine, 52(15), 3336–3348.
